comments.body:
**Scope note from #637's re-plan (2026-09-12): the orphan-identity migration gate (X92) now belongs to this issue.** No #637 slice carries it any more.

**Why here.** 0016 makes the gate a precondition for turning on "the new retirement paths" (`0016:1259-1273`), the identity-keyed retirement paths. This issue is the one that turns them on: it routes supersede and unlink through `retire:bytes:`, and its drain is the first writer of marks that carry an event identity. Before this lands, nothing writes such a mark, so a gate in #637 would have protected nothing.

**What that adds to this slice:**
- the page-wise cleanup pass that re-stamps or drops a mark found on a still-referenced fragment (`0016:1249-1258`), and the durable "orphan-identity cleanup complete" marker it writes when it finishes;
- the identity-keyed paths stay disabled until that marker is observed, falling back to 0016's fail-safe arm.

**One trap to avoid, found in #637's first attempt.** That cleanup dropped a lapsed legacy mark whenever *any* `part:` record still named the fragment, including a published part waiting for its records-mode `retire:records:{parts}` drain, which writes no marks. The failing sequence: an upload publishes; the object is then deleted by `unlink`, which writes legacy marks; a GC pass drops those marks as stale; the part record retires. The fragments were left with no mark and no reference, so nothing would ever reclaim them. 0016 allows "re-stamps or drops" (`0016:1255`). Re-stamp in that case, or drop only against committed references.

**What #637's slices give this issue to build on:**
- #661 walks the `orphan:` ledger in pages under a per-pass budget;
- #662 decodes all three mark shapes (legacy decimal, `{orphaned_at_millis, event}`, `{…, reclaiming: true}`), records reclaim intent before deleting, and adds keyed protection while a `retire:bytes:` obligation is pending (X97).

**Gap: what the drain does with a cancelled upload's untrusted staged record.**

The second bullet says `reclaim_owned` works "with a validated `StagedPlacement`". That is right: the discontinued patch decoded `RS(0,0)`, marked nothing, and deleted the only record naming the bytes. But the issue doesn't say what the drain does with a record that **fails** validation. That case will reach it.

**Where it comes from.** #803 made GC and restore treat two kinds of staged record as untrusted (`crates/custodian/src/gc.rs:656-659` on `main` @ `f41e9c5`):

- a staged placement whose length is not its scheme's fragment count;
- an owned `sidx:` value that will not decode, under a key that still names its chunk.

For either, GC and restore keep **every** fragment of that chunk, on every server (`gc.rs:693-694`). That is correct while the upload is live. Once the upload is cancelled, those bytes are garbage. After a metadata restore, #809 moves every session the restore brought back to `Aborting` and installs its `retire:bytes` obligation. So the drain will meet these records on dead uploads.

**Both obvious behaviours go wrong.**

- **Skip the record:** it stays forever, so every fragment of its chunk stays on disk. For an `sidx:` entry, the terminal delete (gated on the session's `sidx:` range being empty) never fires, so the session record and its `mpuctl` slot stay too. After #808, an untrusted staged record also blocks every drain in the cluster, the way a malformed committed placement already does (`crates/custodian/src/desired_state.rs:234-246`). No automatic path ends any of this.
- **Delete it without marking:** this repeats the discontinued patch's failure, leaving bytes that are unreferenced and never marked.

**Proposed rule.** For a session in `Aborting` only, retire an untrusted record by **chunk id** instead of by placement:

1. Mark `orphan:` on every fragment carrying that chunk id, found from the fleet's fragment listings (a `FragmentId` carries its chunk), not from the untrusted placement.
2. Then delete the record, in the same mark-then-delete order `retire:bytes` already means.

For an `Open` session nothing changes: the record keeps holding its chunk.

**Why this is safe.**

- The upload is dead, so its bytes are garbage whatever the record says. The bad placement only makes the fragments harder to find.
- Upload chunk ids are minted by the gateway at random and never reused (`0016:829`, allocator row).
- GC still checks every fragment against the reference set before it reclaims anything, and waits out the grace period. A fragment that another valid record names is kept.

**Suggested acceptance legs.**

- An `Aborting` session holding a `part:` record with a wrong-length placement, and another holding an `sidx:` entry whose value will not decode. After the drain, and a GC pass past grace:
  - every fragment of both chunks is gone;
  - both records are gone;
  - the terminal delete has fired, and `mpuctl.count` has gone down exactly once per session.
- Control: an `Open` session with the same kind of record keeps every fragment of its chunk, and its record.
- Control: a committed object's fragments on the same servers are untouched.

**Open points.**

- Cost: finding fragments by chunk id needs a fleet listing. Can the drain reuse the one GC already takes each pass?
- Can any feature (copy, dedup) make two objects share a chunk id? GC's re-check covers that case, but it's worth knowing.

**Context.** The rule behind this — keep-on-doubt protects user data, not system residue — is being written into ADR-0045 decision 3 in #811. #809's restore report will name these records (`staged_untrusted`) without flagging them as needing a human. It deliberately promises no automatic cleanup until this issue decides the rule.

milestone.title: 0.1 Alpha
milestone.description: First tagged release (Alpha). Scheduled after the two production-metadata milestones complete: #14 (Metadata Store FoundationDB) and #5 (M4 — Production metadata backend) — i.e. after the FDB go/no-go (#442) records go, the default flips to FDB, and TiKV development stands down (#443). No due date yet; it follows those two. Starts empty as the release marker.
